problem: Avangrid builds its wires for the system's top few hours, but the pipeline picks battery homes by its own sample peak. It picks homes that stay loaded for hours, which is the flat, long shape Scott says a battery cannot cover. Nobody can yet say how many system top hours a given battery home would actually cut.
specific_user: Scott, Avangrid's Program Director of Load Research. He sets the load-shape threshold that decides which homes count as battery and flexibility candidates, and he reports how much of the top 20 to 50 system hours a program can remove. Next in line is the Customer Programs and Products Manager, who sends the battery offer, the managed-charging offer or the thermostat offer to each home on that list.
title: System-Peak Battery Fit Score
solution: The tool takes three inputs: the existing 25,653-home by 8,760-hour AMI matrix, the existing weather join, and one new supporting dataset, the public NYISO hourly zonal load for September 2025 to August 2026. It uses that load to define the system's top 20, 50 and 100 hours, checked against the peak dates Scott gave. For each home it simulates the program battery (2x IQ 10C, 20.16 kWh, 7.68 kW) charging off-peak and discharging into those hours. It scores the kW the battery delivers in system top hours and the share of the home's top-hour load it covers. A peaky home scores high and a flat-high home scores low. It also checks whether one unit is enough. A supply curve (MW in system top hours against homes added) sets the threshold, as Scott asked for: a rule, with the list it produces. Each home also gets a routing column from the existing classes. EV-driven top-hour load goes to managed charging, summer AC load goes to the summer thermostat program, and winter electric-heat load goes to the battery, because a winter thermostat offer is a hard sell. The score runs on one home at a time against a shared list of hours, so it splits by customer shard and scales to the full customer base. The ingest runtime is measured.
evidence: bess.candidates.count = 4,079 homes, picked as 'loaded at least 3.5 kW through the season's event hours on 9 of 10 event days' (readout.txt). That is the persistent, flat-high shape Scott says a battery covers poorly [02:40].

bess.size.two_units = 4,079 and bess.size.one_unit = 0 homes; bess.simple_payback_low_yr = 23.0 and bess.simple_payback_high_yr = 33.0 years against a 15-year warranty (facts.json, readout.txt; prices are assumption.*). This is the economics a peakier, one-unit selection would need to beat.

insight.winter_peak_when = 2026-02-08 17:00, while Scott gives February 7 as the system winter peak [11:41-12:02]; bess.event_window_winter_hours = 17:00-21:00 on the sample's top day (facts.json). The current winter window sits on a different day from the system's peak.

bess.supply_curve.top1000_winter_mw = 4.43 MW vs top1000_summer_mw = 2.72 MW (facts.json). Batteries already carry more in winter, where Scott doubts thermostat programs [08:03], so the battery belongs there.

From hour 8 to 16, Person A measures the per-shard runtime at 25,653 homes and at 10x synthetic copies. Person B, hours 1 to 16: add a dispatch simulation to bess.py, a greedy daily schedule with a 7.68 kW cap and 20.16 kWh of energy, charging off-peak or from solar surplus. It covers one unit and two units, computes coverage share and MW in top-N hours, builds a supply curve for picking the threshold, and fills the routing column from the existing class labels (EV L2, AC, electric heat). Cut order if the team is behind: the 10x scale benchmark first, then the routing column, then the one-unit sizing. The NYISO top-hours join and the dispatch-based coverage score are never cut.
biggest_risk: Every team heard Scott ask for peaky shapes and top hours, so a peakiness-ratio battery list will be common. Our edge rests on the NYISO system-hours join and the dispatch-based coverage score. If the NYISO fetch or the zone mapping fails (customer zones are not in the data), that edge shrinks to the sample aggregate plus two dates. A second risk: the hourly data hides sub-hour peaks, so peaky homes may look more battery-coverable than they are. The deck must say so.

Soft: hourly kWh hides sub-hour peaks, so the coverage share and the 3 kVA status are optimistic. That is already a known limitation in the README and has to go on a slide.
Soft: the threshold is a judgment call read off the supply curve. Scott has not given a target MW, so the knee of the curve has to be stated as the team's rule.

problem: Avangrid pays heat-pump rebates without knowing how much winter peak load each one adds, because meter data cannot yet tell whole-home electric heat from supplemental heat. The winter thermostat program now under discussion may shed almost nothing in the coldest hours, which are the hours the grid is built for.
specific_user: Scott, Program Director of Load Research and one of the judges. He decides how many winter kW each heat-pump rebate adds to the load forecast and which winter flexibility resource his team backs: the proposed winter thermostat program, EV managed charging, or batteries paired with rebates. The Customer Programs and Products Manager and the Director of Advanced Load Forecasting act on the same numbers.
title: What a Heat-Pump Rebate Adds
solution: The inputs are the existing 25,653-home by 8,760-hour matrix, hourly temperature, the heat-pump rebate sample and the current class labels. First, the tool picks the top 20, 50 and 100 system hours in each season and checks them against the system peak dates Scott gave: 2 July for summer and 7 February for winter. Second, it fits each home's kW-versus-temperature curve below 60F and sorts electric-heat homes by curve shape: straight-line whole-home resistance, a curve that bends upward in deep cold (a heat pump with strip backup), or a small, flat response (supplemental or occupancy-driven heat). It checks these labels against the rebate homes. Third, it measures what a rebated heat pump really adds in the winter top hours, using rebate homes against matched non-electric homes with the same cooling signature, split by curve shape. That number replaces the single-hour 3.29 kW and gives a flip count with a range. Fourth, it scores three winter flexibility options on the same top hours: a thermostat setback (sheds little in homes whose curve flattens at the coldest hours, because the heat is already running flat out), shifting the EV Level 2 load that falls in those hours, and winter battery relief from the peaky homes already ranked. The output is one table of kW added per rebate type, conversions to a winter peak, and the cheapest flexibility that covers it, plus a per-home heat-type column in customer_classes.csv.

build_plan_24h: Person A, hours 0 to 10: adds a top-N hours module to segment.py (N = 20, 50 and 100, both seasons, marking 7 and 8 February and 2 July). A then adds a per-home hinge fit of kW against temperature below 60F to features.py: slope in mild cold, slope below about 15F, and overnight share. From those, A labels each electric-heat home as resistance, heat pump with backup, or supplemental, and checks the labels against the rebate sample. Hours 10 to 16: A measures kW added per rebate in the winter top-N hours by curve type against matched non-electric AC homes, and records the increment and a flip-count range in facts.json. Person B, hours 0 to 14: in bess.py, B scores winter flexibility on the same top-N hours. That means the share of electric-heat homes whose curve flattens in the coldest hours (thermostat shed bound), the EV Level 2 kW in winter top hours that could be shifted inside a 24-hour window, and winter relief from the existing battery ranking limited to peaky homes. B swaps the 33% winter placeholder for the measured bound. Person C, hours 0 to 24: keeps the existing Part 1 to 3 slides and adds 3 lead slides: kW per rebate by heat type, top-N winter flexibility scored side by side, and the decision table with the conversion count to a winter peak. C wires every new number through the existing trace check. All three integrate and run make check in hours 16 to 24.
biggest_risk: The curve shapes may not separate. The pipeline already found that listed heat-pump and resistance homes share one median kW-versus-temperature curve, only 10 labeled heat-pump homes are hits, and there is no gas-service flag to confirm supplemental heat. One winter also gives only a handful of hours near the 2.1F peak to test thermostat saturation. To manage this, we report every result as a range and anchor the increment on the rebate list itself, which needs no classifier. If the split fails, we say so plainly: the meters can show X but not Y, and the gas-service flag is the one field that would settle it. That is still an answer to the problem Scott says his team has not solved.

blockers: No soft blocker on the core number: the heat-pump label list has only 60 homes in the 25,653 that remain after the duplicate zip is dropped, and only 24 of them are flagged electric heat. Splitting that by curve shape leaves about 20 homes per bin, so the per-type increments need bootstrap ranges. The pooled rebate increment can be measured either way: a quick probe gives a median of 2.52 kW in the winter top-100 hours against 1.09 kW for non-electric AC homes, about 1.4 kW, compared with today's 3.29 kW from a single hour.

There is no program or upgrade cost data, so 'cheapest flexibility' cannot be stated in dollars. The options should be ranked by kW covered in the winter top-N hours. Any dollar figure goes under assumption.*, which the existing checker already enforces.

There is no gas-service flag, so supplemental heat cannot be confirmed. The classifier already reports that listed heat-pump homes and resistance homes share one median curve (heat_pump confidence is low, with 10 labeled hits), so the three-way curve split may not separate.
Only a handful of winter hours fall near the 2.1F peak, so thermostat saturation rests on a few hours and has to be shown as a bound.
The peak-date check: the data's winter peak is 2026-02-08 17:00, not 7 February. The proposal already marks both 7 and 8 February, so this is a finding to report, not a blocker.
feas.fallback: Lead with the method that needs no classifier. Measure the kW added per heat-pump home on the 60-home label list against matched non-electric AC homes in the top 20, 50 and 100 winter hours, with a bootstrap range. Recompute the flip count (16.8 MW gap divided by that increment) as a range, replacing the single-hour 3.29 kW and 5,100 homes. Put EV Level 2 shiftable kW and battery winter relief (already in facts.json: 2.25, 4.43 and 7.45 MW for the top 500, 1,000 and 2,000 homes) side by side on the same hours, with the thermostat shown as a bound from the coldest-hour flattening share of electric-heat homes. If the resistance, heat-pump-with-backup and supplemental split does not separate, publish that result as 'the meters can show the pooled increment but not the heat type; a gas-service flag would settle it' and drop the per-type column from customer_classes.csv.
